Bangladesh Imposes Temporary Import Tariff Hike on Car Parts, Impacting Local Automotive Industry

The government of Bangladesh has introduced a significant temporary increase in import tariffs on automotive components, a move that has begun to ripple through the country’s automotive manufacturing and assembly sector. The new policy, which took effect last week, raises import duties on key vehicle parts by up to 25 percent, according to an official notice from the National Board of Revenue (NBR).

The measure, described by the Ministry of Commerce as a “short-term response to currency pressures and the need to protect domestic industries,” has already prompted concern among automakers and suppliers. Local manufacturers, who rely heavily on imported kits and parts for assembly, report immediate effects on production costs and supply chains.

ACI Ltd, one of the country’s major automotive assemblers, confirmed that it has slowed production at its Gazipur plant due to rising costs and shipment delays. “We’re seeing a sharp increase in the landed cost of components, which is making it extremely challenging to maintain our current output levels,” said Anwarul Haque, head of operations at ACI Ltd. “Unless the tariffs are revised or supply chains stabilize, we may have to consider further adjustments to our production schedule.”

Industry observers say the tariff hike is likely to cause price increases for locally assembled vehicles in the coming weeks. According to the Bangladesh Automobile Manufacturers Association (BAMA), the cost of assembling a standard sedan could rise by up to 18 percent if the policy remains in place through the quarter.

“We understand the government’s need to address foreign exchange issues,” said BAMA Secretary General Rashed Chowdhury, “but the abrupt increase in tariffs is a major challenge for assemblers and distributors. There’s a risk that this will ultimately be passed on to consumers.”

Officials from the NBR have indicated that the tariff hike is under ongoing review, but declined to comment on when it might be lifted. In the meantime, local companies such as ACI Ltd and Bengal Motors are reassessing their supply and pricing strategies.

Union representatives at several automotive plants voiced concerns over job security if production levels continue to fall. “Our members are anxious,” said Shafiqul Islam, a union leader at a Dhaka assembly facility. “We hope the authorities will consider the impact on workers and the sector as a whole.”
